Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drift off into a world of my own
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
There is something wrong with me as a person

vignette:
Amina is a 25-year-old nurse who came to treatment months after leaving a war zone, where she had been a civilian caught in repeated episodes of violence and threat. When she speaks about that period, she does not offer a smooth account. The parts she can convey come in sharp, painful fragments: running at night after shelling began nearby, the crush of bodies in makeshift shelter, the sound of people crying out and the helplessness of seeing the wounded without having the equipment or safety to care for them. What stands out most in the way she holds the experience now is not only fear, but a deep sense of degradation. She has come to believe that what happened exposed something shameful and broken in her. In her mind, surviving those moments while terrified, disoriented, and unable to help everyone who needed help feels less like an understandable human response and more like evidence that she is inadequate.

After she arrived in the United States and resumed work as a nurse, the memories did not settle into the past. Instead, when they came, they arrived with such force that she felt pulled back into the war zone as if the present had dropped away. In session she described moments in which remembering did not feel like remembering at all; it felt as though she was there again, with her body tightening and her attention narrowing until the room around her became hard to register. When this happened, she would become so emotionally flooded that she had to stop what she was doing, sometimes stepping away and sitting in silence until the wave passed. Along with the fear and intensity, there was grief so large that she struggled to put words around it. The memories were bound up with losses she could barely tolerate touching. Even a brief return of the images could leave her feeling shattered for the rest of the day.

Because of this, Amina has built her days around not getting too close to the event in her mind. She tries not to think about it deliberately, and if she feels a memory beginning at the edges of awareness she shifts quickly, focusing on a task, a screen, or some small practical detail. When that does not work, she drifts away internally into elaborate private fantasy, disappearing into a world of her own for a few moments or longer. She knows this is happening; she describes it as slipping out of reach of everything around her. At work, during quieter parts of a hospital shift, she can find herself staring at a monitor or supply cart while her mind moves somewhere far removed from the unit. The habit gives her temporary distance from what feels unbearable, but it also leaves her embarrassed when a coworker has to repeat a question or when she realizes she has missed part of a handoff.

She also avoids talking about the war and its aftermath with almost everyone, including her partner. When he has asked what it was really like, or why she seems suddenly far away on certain evenings, she has shut the conversation down with a brief “I don’t want to get into it.” The idea of speaking it aloud feels dangerous to her, as though words might make the memories fully present and uncontrollable. There is shame in it too. She is certain that if she were to describe what happened and how she reacted, other people would see what she already believes about herself: that she is not strong enough, that something is wrong with her as a person, that she carries a permanent humiliation she cannot undo. She does not speak this belief casually; it sits close to the center of how she now understands herself.

Over time these habits have narrowed her life. Her partner experiences her as present one moment and unreachable the next, and Amina feels guilty about that distance while still insisting to herself that silence is safer. At work she continues to function and remains committed to nursing, but the emotional effort of keeping memories pushed back leaves her drained. The contrast between the competent young nurse others see and the defective person she believes herself to be has become harder for her to bear.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a single crisis but the recognition that she could no longer contain the war by refusing to think or speak about it. The memories still break through, and when they do, she feels overwhelmed and overcome with grief. She came to therapy frightened that if she lets herself remember fully, she will be consumed by it, and frightened too that the humiliation she feels will never lift. At the same time, beneath her caution, there is a hope that she might one day be able to recall what happened without feeling as though she is living it again, and without concluding each time that the event revealed something irreparably wrong with who she is.
